title: Second-line oncology launch and Veeva multichannel strategy
challenge: A new therapy entering a class with three established competitors and very similar headline data.
audience: Haematologists and specialist nurses in five European markets.
work: Advisory boards to find the unmet need competitors had missed, a positioning built around it and a multichannel launch campaign built in Veeva.
outcome: A shared story that marketing, medical and sales can adapt for approval in each launch market.

title: Immunology brand repositioning and HCP education in IBD
challenge: A trusted brand losing share to newer options despite strong long-term evidence.
work: Research into why prescribers were switching, a refreshed value story and a peer-to-peer programme led by respected clinicians.
outcome: A clear reason to keep talking about the brand and a programme designed to expand into further markets.

title: Rare disease patient support and treatment adherence
challenge: Patients on a complex treatment regimen were dropping off in the first months.
audience: Patients, carers and the small group of specialist centres that treat them.
work: Interviews with patients and carers, then a support programme and counselling tools built around the moments people found hardest.
outcome: Materials specialist nurses can use in clinic and a programme designed to grow with the patient community.

title: What does the evidence actually let you say?
summary: A practical edit for the moment when a clear sentence starts promising more than the study can support.

example.original: The support programme improved treatment adherence.
example.revision: In an observational study, people who chose to join the support programme recorded fewer missed doses over 12 weeks.
example.note: This fictional example shows the difference between an observed association and a claim of cause. The revised line keeps the study design, self-selection and timeframe visible.

sections.heading: Start with the claim
sections.text: Put the sentence next to the source that supports it. Circle the verb. “Improved”, “prevented” and “was associated with” describe different things. If the verb is stronger than the study design allows, a shorter sentence only makes the problem easier to miss.

sections.heading: Keep the comparison in view
sections.text: Ask whether someone reading a screenshot could tell what was measured, for whom and against what. Put the detail that changes the interpretation beside the claim, where it can do its job.

sections.heading: Edit for the reader’s next decision
sections.text: Read the line aloud and ask a colleague to explain it back to you. Their version will tell you which qualification disappeared. Put that qualification back into the main sentence and try again.

title: The first five minutes of a launch brief
summary: Three questions to get the team talking about the decision in front of them before the channel plan takes over.

sections.heading: Whose decision are we trying to change?
sections.text: Name one person, one moment and one decision. “Oncologists need awareness” leaves most of the work to the reader. “A specialist deciding what to discuss after a patient’s first treatment stops working” gives the team a situation they can investigate.

sections.heading: What happens today?
sections.text: Ask for a recent example. When did someone make that decision? What was in front of them? Who else had a say? A description of what happens today gives you something to test before you invest in a campaign.

sections.heading: Which unknown would change the plan?
sections.text: Write it down and agree how to investigate it. If the answer would change the audience, language or timing, it belongs in the research brief before production starts.

title: Give the AI draft a reading test
summary: A simple way to review AI-assisted copy when the wording sounds plausible and the source still has the final say.

sections.heading: Give the review a small job
sections.text: Choose one paragraph and the approved material it draws on. Ask the reviewer to mark each factual phrase and find the passage that supports it. A complete-looking paragraph becomes a set of checkable statements.

sections.heading: Look at the joins
sections.text: Pay particular attention to phrases such as “so”, “therefore” and “which means”. They can turn two accurate sentences into an inference the source never made. Check the connection as carefully as you check the facts.

sections.heading: Keep the edit attached to the evidence
sections.text: Record the source passage and the reason for each substantive change in your existing review workflow. The next reviewer can then see what changed and why, even when they were never part of the drafting conversation.

title: Shape the story
body: The decisions made before launch set the course for years. We help you understand the market, test the idea with the people who matter and land the positioning and core claims that everything else will build on.

title: Make the first impression count
body: You only get one launch. We've worked on more than 50, including complex cell therapy launches, so we know where the time goes and where the approval risks sit.

title: Find new reasons to talk
body: New indications, new audiences, new data. We help brands keep the story fresh without losing what made it work.

title: Defend what you've built
body: A competitor launches. A biosimilar arrives. Exclusivity ends. We've helped brands through all three, and given some twenty-year-old brands a new lease of life along the way.

title: Support patients beyond the prescription
body: The work doesn't stop at the prescription. We create support programmes and tools that help people understand their treatment and stay on it.

name: Oncology and haematology
challenge: Fast-moving data, complex mechanisms and treatment decisions with very high stakes.
experience: CAR-T and cell therapy launches, leukaemias, lymphomas, myeloma, breast, lung and prostate cancer.

name: Immunology
challenge: Many treatment options, and patients who have often tried several already.
experience: Crohn's and ulcerative colitis, lupus, psoriatic and rheumatoid arthritis, HLH.

name: Neurology
challenge: Long journeys, outcomes that are hard to measure and carers who are part of every decision.
experience: Multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's, Alzheimer's, epilepsy, migraine, post-stroke spasticity.

name: Rare disease
challenge: Small populations, few specialists and every word under scrutiny.
experience: Gaucher disease, acromegaly, primary HLH, beta thalassaemia, haemophilia.

name: Medical devices
challenge: Audiences who buy on evidence and technique, not mechanism of action.
experience: Biosurgery, fibrin sealants, haemostatic matrices, surgery and wound care.
